extracted.intended_audience: teachers, school administrators, education reformers, and policy makers interested in industrial education (and secondarily mineralogists/field geologists reading the journal)
extracted.subtask_short: industrial education curriculum for public schools
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance for designing and delivering industrial education in public schools: what students should acquire (disposition, knowledge, powers), how schools should structure curriculum and pedagogy, and practical classroom/field methods. Also includes related guidance for mineralogical fieldwork and scientific collaboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial education should be universal
rubrics_metrics.description: All education should be industrial, and everybody should be industrially educated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues it is a tenable proposition that industrial education should be universal; motivates curriculum design choices that serve broad citizenship and adaptability in changing industries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three core elements of industrial education
rubrics_metrics.description: An industrially educated person must possess: (1) an industrial disposition, (2) industrial knowledge, and (3) industrial power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three elements together form the observable aims of industrial education and should guide school objectives and assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: An industrial disposition leads to a cheerful and even happy devotion to some chosen employment as the avenue to contribute to the world's wealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schools should foster the creative/producing instinct from childhood (play as 'embryo industries'), carrying forward delight in producing into mature industry; cultivate duty, benevolence, and pride in work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: General and special knowledge which will put the pupil in possession of the best human experience in the direction of his chosen vocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schools must make a wise selection from accumulated knowledge to enable students to choose which industrial 'height' to climb, to facilitate transitions between industries, and to build intelligent sympathy among different worker classes (including political/economic relations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial power (overall)
rubrics_metrics.description: A development of physical, intellectual, and artistic power to reduce chances of failure and give a just consciousness of strength enabling hopeful, successful work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industrial power is subdivided into physical, intellectual, and artistic power — each requiring targeted curriculum and instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical power
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop a body capable of enduring the strains and fatigues likely in ordinary life and work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schools should apply the best physiological knowledge of the age to physical education and health practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual power
rubrics_metrics.description: Impart knowledge according to the laws of mental assimilation so mental dyspepsia is avoided and the pupil can quickly and accurately solve ordinary life problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction should follow modern understanding of mental growth; avoid overcrowding subjects that cause poor assimilation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic power
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop the sense of the beautiful to give finesse and finish to whatever work the pupil undertakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage artistic feeling in all work (whether farming, tailoring, building, or painting) so the workman has an artist's sense and the artist is recognized as a working-man.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schools should be preparatory (not specialist vocational training)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public schools should form the road leading up to the base of special schools rather than attempt to train specialists (e.g., physicians, lawyers, artists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public schools provide foundational industrial knowledge and power; specialized institutions should fit students for climbing particular industrial heights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wise selection and reduction of subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not multiply subjects in the curriculum; reduce and wisely choose subjects to conserve children's energies and avoid superficial learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid fragmenting broad departments into many petty fields; teach closely connected lines together so teacher and pupil gain vigor and freedom through coherent study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial knowledge defined (materials, processes, relations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Industrial knowledge consists of acquaintance with industrial materials, processes, and relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Materials: natural forces and substances from mineral, vegetable, animal worlds. Processes: operations converting crude materials into useful forms. Relations: mechanism of exchange and considerations of political economy. Use this taxonomy to plan content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foster industrial instinct from early childhood
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize the industrial instinct as a creative instinct manifest in children's play; cultivate it into mature productive impulses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use play, blocks, and early production activities to nurture the joy of producing; connect early creative play to later industrial occupations and civic duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use common industrial materials and varied concrete objects in arithmetic
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace abstract objects with real industrial materials (beans, corn, fragments from trades, leaves, rocks, fabrics) to teach number and operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using many kinds of objects sustains interest, trains observation and classification, and simultaneously imparts industrial knowledge (e.g., recognition of useful trees, rocks, ores, textiles). Arrange samples for wall reference; source fragments from local craftsmen at no cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach measures, weights, and money integrated with arithmetic
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures, weights, and money can be taught more efficiently alongside early arithmetic instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce dimensions (inch, foot, yard, square/cubic measures), use either French (metric) or English measures, and perform additions/subtractions with objects of definite dimensions to build sense of proportion and measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop sense of dimension and proportion through measurement and drawing
rubrics_metrics.description: Constant drawing and measurement (schoolroom, objects, body parts) cultivates a sense of dimension and proportion crucial for mechanical and artistic drawing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early crude sketches progressing to more perfect representations form a foundation for mechanical and artistic skills essential to many industries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach color mixing and develop color-sense early
rubrics_metrics.description: Children should learn to mix paints and represent simpler hues, which develops color-sense and detects color-blindness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use color exercises tied to plants, animals, rocks, and sky; this supports later industrial applications requiring accurate color perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate arithmetic with simple scientific apparatus and political economy
rubrics_metrics.description: Advanced ratio and proportion instruction should use simple scientific experiments and materials that illustrate scientific laws and principles of political economy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use apparatus (exhibition or shop-made) to demonstrate levers, pendulum vibrations, musical scale frequencies, and economic examples so students see practical mission of ratio/proportion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral/conscience development must preside over knowledge and powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Over all knowledge and power a conscience should decide 'ought' and 'ought not' loudly enough to be obeyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral education should be woven into ordinary subjects so students apply industrial skills with conscientious regard for rights of others and civic responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use variety of objects to train observation and classification
rubrics_metrics.description: A great variety of objects in teaching number sustains interest and trains observing powers to make distinctions and classify things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Switching classes of objects (blocks, leaves, fabrics, ores) improves engagement and perceptual training; follows principles advocated by various pedagogues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use local artisans' shop materials as free educational resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Fragments from local trades (tailor, milliner, upholsterer) supply needed materials for classroom instruction at no cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Samples can be arranged artistically on boards and hung for constant reference and review to support arithmetic and industrial-knowledge lessons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field observation essential for mineralogical/earth science study
rubrics_metrics.description: Mineralogists should devote more time to personal observation in the field and study the order and manner of occurrence of minerals in place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying solely on cabinet specimens is insufficient; careful inspection of quarries and mines and observations on manner of occurrence provide rich scientific material; geological surveys should direct competent observers into the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mineralogy requires union of physical, geometrical, and chemical properties
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine the true character of a mineral a union of all physical, geometrical (crystallography), and chemical properties is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern mineralogy should combine crystallography (form), chemistry (composition), and physical characters; investigators must apply results from physics, geology, and chemistry and cooperate with specialists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate origin, associations, transformations, and causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Mineralogical investigations must include history of origin, relations to associated species, changes undergone, and causes/results of these changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These topics require geology and chemistry input; a broader foundation is needed than earlier eras of mineralogy that focused only on external characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geological surveys should support scientific mineralogy not only ore discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: State and national geological surveys must do more than guide to useful ores; they should perform scientific observations on mineral constituents and modes of occurrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveys should direct competent persons to observe both main constituents and manner of occurrence, and carefully inspect quarries and mines to prevent loss of valuable scientific material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic exploration preferred to accidental discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Many interesting mineral discoveries have been the result of accident rather than systematic exploration; more systematic, intelligent exploration is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage trained mineralogists to spend time in the field and wealthy amateurs to fund local exploration rather than importing foreign specimens.
